title: Specificity
body:
$$
\text{Specificity} = \frac{\text{TN}}{\text{TN} + \text{FP}}
$$

**Of the things that really were negative, what fraction did you correctly leave alone?** The
mirror image of [[Sensitivity]], computed down the other truth column of the
[[Confusion Matrix]]. Also called the true negative rate, and $1 - \text{specificity}$ is the false
positive rate, which is what an ROC curve puts on its $x$ axis.

**In [[STATISTICS]] this is $1 - \alpha$.** See [[Type I and Type II Errors]].

Like [[Sensitivity]] it is a within-column rate, so it does not move when the class balance
changes. That is the property both metrics exist for. What it is *not* is the negative predictive
value $\text{TN}/(\text{TN}+\text{FN})$, which reads across the prediction row instead and does
depend on the base rate: same relationship as recall to precision, one column down.

The pair is what a threshold trades against. Demanding more evidence before calling positive raises
this and lowers [[Sensitivity]]; loosening does the reverse. Where to sit on that curve is decided
by which error costs more, which is a domain question. A screening test deliberately runs low
specificity to keep [[False Negative|misses]] near zero, and accepts the follow-up load.

**High specificity is not enough on rare positives.** 99% specificity sounds excellent, but at a
1-in-1000 base rate it still yields about ten [[False Positive|false positives]] per true one, so
precision collapses. That arithmetic is [[Bayes Theorem]]'s.
